en: Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zhi of Changshui, Part Five:
Realization through Returning the Hearing to its Source. This section follows the sequence of the previous chapter on Aniruddha, as it concerns the faculty of hearing among the six sense organs.
Now, I shall joyfully expound upon the meaning of perfect penetration in detail.
Subsequently, the Emperor issued an edict to select the "Linked Rings" (Lianhuan), which was therefore explained last to signify that it represents the ultimate reality.
Had it been explained earlier, the Buddhas would have emitted light to celebrate and praise this gate, rendering the other sages' efforts superfluous.

If one does not offer praise and commendation, this gateway will not be manifested as the true *āyatana* of perfect penetration; therefore, the current section is titled "Returning the Hearing to Reality.
The text has two parts:
first, the formal presentation of cultivation and realization, which has three sub-sections: [The text continues with the three sub-sections.]
I. A formal account of the causes for cultivation, in two parts:
1. Encountering the Buddha and receiving his teachings.
At that time, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I recall that in the past, incalculable kalpas ago as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there appeared in the world a Buddha named Avalokiteśvara.
Under that Buddha, I gave rise to the bodhicitta; he taught me to enter samādhi through hearing, contemplation, and cultivation.”

The Brahma-sound name is Anavalokitêśvara, which is translated here as Guānshìyīn (Avalokiteśvara); this name is established based on the relationship between the subject and object, or the wisdom and its objective realm.
Whether encountering the Buddha or contemplating the Dharma, all serve as his teachers; thus, in the succession from teacher to disciple, there is no contradiction.

The general path of all practices consists of the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation; there is not a single Buddha who does not transform sentient beings through sound, nor a single capacity that does not attain understanding and realization by hearing the teachings through the faculty of the ear; it is for this reason that the teaching of that Buddha enters through this [faculty].
2. Cultivating contemplation according to the teaching:
"First, within hearing, one enters the flow and loses the object; once that which is entered has become still, the two characteristics of movement and stillness clearly cease to arise."
"In this way, as it gradually increases, that which is heard and that which hears both come to an end.
"Entering the stream" is like reversing the flow.

Initially, one contemplates the nature of hearing, reflecting back to remain detached from conditions, and no longer following the arising and ceasing of the shifting sensory objects before one; therefore, it is said that "entering the stream, the object is lost."

Because the characteristics of the sound-object are not followed, they remain quiescent and do not arise; for arising is movement. Since the characteristic of movement has vanished, stillness likewise does not arise, because the objects of movement and stillness are what the faculty of hearing perceives.

Now, observing that the absence of intrinsic nature is fundamentally non-existent and ultimately unattainable, it is said that "it is clearly and vividly unarisen"; this refers to the signlessness of the grasped object (*grāhya-nimitta*).
The *Awakening of Faith* states: "One should remain far removed from all illusory and false realms."

Furthermore, as one increases the practice of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), once the objects of perception have vanished and the characteristics of hearing do not arise, this very characteristic of being able to hear is itself the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*). Since both the subject (the ability to hear) and the object (that which is heard) are simultaneously stilled, it is said that "hearing and what is heard are exhausted"; this refers to the elimination of the wisdom of hearing.

If this is so for one faculty, it is likewise for all other faculties; this is also what was previously stated in the text as "this faculty first attaining liberation, first realizing the emptiness of persons.
The *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* says: "That which is like an illusion in the mind is also to be transcended."
"Exhausting hearing so that it does not abide, one realizes that which is perceived is empty.
The locus where hearing is exhausted is the essence of the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*), which is termed "realization" (*bodha*).
This wisdom of realization belongs to the sixth consciousness; thus, one abandons hearing and contemplates the meaning.

Now, one does not dwell even in this state of "hearing to the end," but further advances in contemplative practice to contemplate and deconstruct both this act of perceiving and the perceived object of hearing; since neither is established, it is called emptiness.
This refers to the elimination of conceptual wisdom (*cintāmayī-prajñā*). As the preceding text states: "The emptiness is perfectly luminous, achieving liberation through the Dharma.
The *Awakening of Mahāśraddhā* (*Śūraṅgama-samādhi*) says: "One distances oneself from illusions, and further distances oneself [from that distancing]."
"The realization of emptiness reaches ultimate perfection, and that which is emptied by emptiness is extinguished.

When the place where emptiness is realized is reached, the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) is exhausted, and one remains solely in correspondence with the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).

As the practice of contemplation increases and becomes subtle, the wisdom of cultivation reaches its ultimate perfection; therefore, it is said that "the realization of emptiness reaches ultimate perfection."
This wisdom of cultivation that can empty and the awakening that is emptied are both non-existent; therefore, it is said that "the emptiness and that which is emptied are extinguished.
This elimination of the wisdom of cultivation is precisely what was described in the preceding passage as "having already attained liberation from dharmas," wherein both are empty and do not arise.
The *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* states: "Depart from that which is free from illusion; depart even from this departure.
"When birth and cessation have ceased, quiescent extinction manifests before one.
When birth and cessation have ceased, this refers back to the three preceding wisdoms, wherein the three emptinesses are fully exhausted.
Since they have been successively shown to be empty and both belong to the realm of arising and ceasing, this point has been reached as the ultimate limit; hence it is said, "having ceased.
The true principle of non-arising and the wondrous nature of quiescent permanence manifest clearly and vividly; hence it is said, "quiescent extinction is present before one."
Therefore, the preceding text states: "This is called the bodhisattva entering the patience of non-arising from samādhi.

This refers to the perfect contemplation of the nature of hearing, wherein there is no external object; one gradually clarifies coarse thoughts and slightly eliminates subtle perceptions until reaching the state of no-thought.

As stated in the preceding passage: "When it is still, deep, and unmoving, the sand and soil naturally settle and pure water appears before one; this is called the initial subduing of adventitious afflictions.
When the mud is removed and only pure water remains, this is called the eternal severance of fundamental ignorance."
When the signs of illumination are pure and refined, all transformations and manifestations do not constitute afflictions; they are all in accord with the wondrous virtue of the purity of Nirvana.
This constitutes the stage from the initial practice of contemplation up to the stage of semblance awakening, which is termed the position of arising and ceasing.
"Entering into partial awakening and realizing the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharmakṣānti) is called the stage of non-arising.
However, this initial realization of the realm is inconceivable and not different from that of a Buddha.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "The initial mind and the ultimate mind are not two; yet between these two minds, the former is more difficult.
After entering this stage, every thought is quiescent and extinguished, naturally flowing into the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge).

This gate of contemplation is precisely the perfect cultivation of the three contemplations within a single mind. Now, by reflecting back from hearing, thinking, and practicing to detach from external conditions and reveal one's own inherent nature of hearing, coarse thoughts do not arise and subtle thoughts do not emerge, leading ultimately to stillness and extinction.
To speak by relying on the principle of emptiness means that when one is empty, all things are empty.
When the nature of hearing manifests and the underlying principle appears therein, it is called "the manifestation of quiescence."
2. Fully Manifesting the Virtues of the Fruit, in two parts:
A. Attaining the Virtues of the Fruit.
"Suddenly transcending the mundane and supramundane worlds, one attains perfect clarity throughout the ten directions and achieves two kinds of excellence: [text continues]"
First, above, it harmonizes with the fundamental, wondrous mind of enlightenment of all Buddhas throughout the ten directions, sharing the same compassionate power as the Buddha-Tathāgatas;
second, below, it harmonizes with all sentient beings of the six realms throughout the ten directions, sharing the same sorrowful longing as all those beings.

The prior manifestation of quiescent extinction is the virtue of severance; the wondrous mind of original enlightenment is the virtue of wisdom; and the two powers of compassion are the virtue of grace.

Since this is the perfect cultivation, the three virtues are perfectly realized; therefore, it transcends both the ordinary worldlings of the mundane realm and the three vehicles of the supramundane. This is the Supreme Vehicle, which only Buddhas and Buddhas can fully exhaust.

Regarding "perfectly luminous in the ten directions": one who realizes this state perceives that throughout the ten dharma-realms and the three worlds, there is nothing that is not suchness and nothing that does not become a Buddha.
Because it is perfect, no virtue is lacking; because it is luminous, no obstruction remains unexhausted.

Unconditioned compassion is the characteristic of the Buddha-mind; being fully endowed with all virtues, it is the foremost of merits. Because it is the most excellent among the excellent dharmas, it is called "extraordinary.

The fundamental wondrous enlightened mind is one's own mind, which is non-dual and perfect with that of all Tathāgatas. Having personally realized this today, it is termed "union"; through union, one attains bliss, and thus shares in the power of compassion.

All sentient beings are likewise this very mind, without duality or distinction; thus they are also conjoined with it. Because they are conjoined, one sees that their fundamental nature is the realization of the Buddha-way, yet they have mistakenly wandered through the cycle of rebirth; therefore, they are objects of both compassion and veneration.

From this point downward, the vision of the lower realms should uproot suffering; all of these flow forth from these two alone. 1. The Declaration:
"World-Honored One!

Because I made offerings to the Tathāgata Avalokiteśvara, I received from that Tathāgata the Vajra Samādhi of Hearing-Perfuming and Hearing-Cultivation, which is like an illusion. Since I share the same power of compassion as the Buddha-Tathāgatas, my body has become capable of thirty-two manifestations as I enter various lands."

By cultivating the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and meditation through the power of illusion-like [samādhi], one accomplishes the vajra-samādhi, which can shatter the subtle ignorance of beginningless time and perfectly realize the essence of the Tathāgatagarbha.
Based on the essence, function arises; responding according to conditions, one enters the bodies of the lands.
As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "The pure and wondrous Dharma-body is serene yet responds to all."

Regarding the statement "thirty-two" mentioned here: it is because the types of beings capable of bringing about [such a body] do not exceed this number; it is not that there is a fixed limit to what is manifested.
Second, the enumeration and explanation has four parts:
the holy body has four [aspects].
First, the Buddha-body:
"World-Honored One!

If there are bodhisattvas who enter samādhi, advance in the cultivation of the outflow-free, and bring their resolute understanding to full manifestation, I manifest the body of a Buddha to preach the Dharma for them, causing them to attain liberation."

A Bodhisattva of the tenth stage, seated upon the Flower King Throne and on the verge of attaining perfect enlightenment, must likewise receive the teachings of a distinct Buddha through hearing and cultivation, so as to sever the final subtle ignorance.
Therefore, Avalokiteśvara manifests as the tenth-level *parabhogakāya* (body of enjoyment for others) and preaches the Dharma for them.

As for "resolute belief" (*adhimukti*), it refers to the patient acceptance and firm retention of a determined object, such that one is not led astray by other conditions; this indicates the moment when the most fundamental non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) is about to reach perfection, and is thus called "resolute belief."

However, once this Bodhisattva has ascended to the stages (*bhūmi*), although they remain in the causal state, they are able to manifest the bodies of higher stages to preach the Dharma for others. Because they have perfectly realized that a single stage is all stages, with no further gradations of depth, they are thus able to manifest them.
2. Pratyekabuddhas:

"If those who are still in training (śaikṣa) attain a state of tranquil, wondrous clarity, and their sublime excellence becomes fully manifest, I appear before them in the form of a pratyekabuddha and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve liberation."

The *kinnara* attains awakening through solitary insight, appearing in an age where no Buddha exists. Disgusted with clamor and delighting in stillness, he dwells alone in the mountains and forests. The two stages of *sambhāra* (provisioning) and *prayoga* (application) are termed "those in training" (*śaikṣa*); thereafter, by severing the afflictions, he realizes the state of "one beyond training" (*aśaikṣa*).
According to the principles of the *svayāna*, when wisdom is about to realize what has not yet been realized, it is called "quiescent, wondrous clarity.
The Bodhisattva manifests in a body similar to that [of the practitioner], first acknowledging their original habits and subsequently causing them to draw near to the Buddha.
Third, the Pratyekabuddhas:

"If there are those in training who sever the twelve links of dependent origination, and through the excellence of that severance, the supreme and wondrous nature manifests in full perfection, I appear before them in the body of a Pratyekabuddha and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to attain liberation."
*Pratyekabuddha* is translated as "Solitary Enlightened One" (*dujue*) and also as "Conditionally Enlightened One" (*yuanjue*).
The former [the *pratyekabuddha*] attains awakening through self-realization alone, whereas the latter attains awakening based on the teachings.

Contemplating the twelve links of dependent origination, they employ two types of contemplative methods: the contemplation of the process of cyclic existence (*pravṛtti*) and the contemplation of its cessation (*nivṛtti*), taking the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*) as the primary gateway.

Before the True [Wisdom] has been awakened, one is called a "learner" (śaikṣa); as their wisdom and principle are about to become perfect, the Bodhisattva’s body manifests in a form identical to theirs to necessarily induce them to advance.
Fourth, regarding the Śrāvakas:

"If there are learners who have attained the emptiness of the Four Noble Truths and enter cessation through the Path of Cultivation, and the Supreme Nature appears perfectly before them, I manifest the body of a Śrāvaka before them and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to attain liberation."
Because they awaken by hearing the teachings on the sounds of the Four Noble Truths, they are called *śrāvakas* (Hearers).
After the realization of truth, those in the three fruits and the three stages leading toward them are all termed "those in training" (*śaikṣa*).

Prior to the realization of truth, while in the stage of patience (*kṣānti*), one employs contaminated wisdom (*sāsrava-jñāna*) to contract the contemplation and observe the Four Noble Truths, performing thirty-two aspects of mental application (*ākāra*). When the sixteen moments of mind of the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*) arise as the uncontaminated path (*anāsrava-mārga*), one severs the eighty-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*) of discriminative afflictions belonging to the Four Noble Truths and realizes the principle of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), which is termed the "emptiness of the Four Noble Truths."

From the stage following the first fruit, one progresses to sever the innate afflictions and realizes the principle of the Truth of Cessation; this is called entering cessation through the Path of Cultivation.
As one is about to ascend to the state of No-More-Learning (aśaikṣa), it is called the "perfect manifestation of the supreme nature."

He manifests his body and preaches the Dharma so that they may swiftly realize it; thereafter, he leads them away from lingering at the "Transformation City" (the *hiraṇyagarbha* city) and causes them to advance toward the Great Fruit.
Second, the celestial nature has two parts:
first, the counterparts of Śakra, Brahmā, and Īśvara.

"If there are sentient beings who desire to awaken their minds, refrain from the defilements of desire, and purify their bodies, I will manifest before them in the form of a Brahmā King and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to attain liberation."

If there are those who possess aspiration, their minds become clear and awakened, their physical radiance becomes pure, and they are born into the fourth dhyāna, undefiled by the dust-like afflictions of the desire realm.

He manifests as a Brahmā King to preach the Dharma of the four dhyānas, explaining the sequence of entering and emerging from the factors of dhyāna and their cultivation and realization, so that they may leave behind desire and be reborn in the Brahma world.

"If there are sentient beings who wish to become lords of the heavens to rule over all the devas, I appear before them in the form of Śakra and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve their goal."

Sentient beings love to preside over the various heavens; the Bodhisattva manifests as Śakra and teaches the ten superior wholesome deeds, causing their roots of precept to be pure, so that they are born at the summit of the earth, dwell in the Sudarśana Palace, and become kings of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.

"If there are sentient beings who desire bodily mastery to travel throughout the ten directions, I manifest before them in the form of a Śakra-devānām-indra and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve their goal."

Desiring mastery over the body to travel throughout the ten directions and manifest in the forms of two classes of devas to preach the Dharma and transform sentient beings—namely, those of the Yāma and Tuṣita heavens—one is called "Mastery" (Vaśavartin). Regarding this, Cien states:
"Having attained the fruit of maturation (vipākaphala), one acts according to one's will, surpassing the two lower heavens."
"The fruits of the two lower heavens are obtained by relying upon trees; now, because they obtain them according to their desires, it is called 'mastery.

If there are sentient beings who desire mastery over their bodies to fly through the void, I manifest before them in the form of Maheśvara and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve this."
The gods of the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations and the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations are called Mahāśvara.

Because they do not delight in the fruits of karmic maturation, but rather delight in transforming both themselves and others into instruments of pleasure for their enjoyment, they are called Mahāśvara.

However, if one were to assign [the gods] solely to the two heavens of Nirmāṇarati and Paranirmita-vaśavartin, the meaning would not be fully encompassed; therefore, following the Ci'en school, all four heavens are included.
Second, the category of the collective subsumption of ghosts and spirits.

"If there are sentient beings who love to command ghosts and spirits and protect their lands, I shall manifest before them in the body of a Great Heavenly General and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve success."

The Celestial Great General is a commander under the jurisdiction of the Lord of Devas; he resides separately in each of the thirty-two heavens, leading spirits and deities to guard and protect the four directions.

"If there are sentient beings who desire to govern the world and protect its inhabitants, I manifest before them in the form of the Four Heavenly Kings and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve their goal."

The Four Heavenly Kings are the foremost of those who ascend and the first heaven of the lower realms; each resides upon one of the terraces of Mount Sumeru. Each King leads two divisions of spirits, totaling eight classes of beings, who protect and guard the boundaries of the realm.

"If there are sentient beings who desire to be born in celestial palaces and command spirits and deities, I manifest before them in the form of a prince of the Four Heavenly Kings' realm and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve their goal."
"The Crown Prince of the Heavenly King refers to those such as Nanda.
Governing and presiding over the administration, he commands spirits and creatures to protect the world and benefit humanity.
The Bodhisattva’s body is identical [to theirs]; first he causes them to achieve accomplishment, and subsequently leads them to weary of and detach from [samsara]."
Third, the stage of human beings, which has three parts.
First, the section on sovereigns, ministers, and subordinates:
"If there are sentient beings who delight in being rulers of men, I manifest before them in the body of a human king and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve fulfillment."
"O King, when one moves toward others, all people will turn toward him.
Just as the kings of the four wheels and the minor kings (kṣudraka-rāja) transform those below through their superior conduct, there is nothing that does not follow them."

"If there are sentient beings who cherish their clan and lineage and are highly esteemed by the world, I manifest before them in the form of an elder and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve fulfillment."
The elder possesses ten virtues:

namely, noble lineage, high rank, great wealth, majestic power, profound wisdom, advanced age, pure conduct, complete etiquette, praise from those above, and the devotion of those below. One who possesses these ten virtues is called a Great Elder.

"If there are sentient beings who delight in discussing names and phrases and dwell in self-purification, I manifest before them in the body of a layperson (*gṛhapati*) and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve fulfillment."

"Extensively learned and possessing a powerful memory, yet not seeking official office; dwelling in great wealth while maintaining integrity and purity of will—therefore he is called a 'Resident' (Upāsaka).

If there are sentient beings who love to govern a realm or adjudicate the affairs of a district, I manifest before them in the body of a minister or official and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve success."
A "guo" (state) is a territorial domain; when large, it is called a "bang" (nation).
A "bang" means to bestow; those who have performed meritorious service are enfeoffed therein.
An "yi" (township) is equivalent to a "xian" (district); each of the five or six officials has their own jurisdiction, all of whom serve as administrative officers.
In this way, they shall repair and govern the state and family, transform their teachings and customs, and exercise decisive judgment so that the people suffer no injustice or oppression.

"If there are sentient beings who love various arts and sciences and seek to protect and sustain themselves, I appear before them in the form of a Brahmin and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve fulfillment."
"Brahmin, what you call 'pure conduct'—incantations, mathematics, arts, and methods of cultivation—are all merely technical skills.
When a Bodhisattva seizes the opportunity to manifest signs and encourages one toward completion, what thing is there that he does not transform?"
2. The Contrast between the Homeless and the Householder:

"If there is a man who delights in learning and has left the household life, upholding the various precepts and regulations, I will manifest before him in the body of a bhikṣu and preach the Dharma for him, enabling him to achieve accomplishment."
*Śīla* means precept (*jie*), and *vinaya* means discipline (*lü*).
Because one relies on the laws of the *vinaya* to prevent what is improper and cease evil, it is called "precept," which refers to the two hundred and fifty precepts.

"If there are women who delight in learning and leave the household life, upholding the various prohibitions and precepts, I will manifest before them in the body of a bhikṣuṇī and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve fulfillment."
The *ni* (nun) possesses a female voice; she is a female bhikṣu who upholds the five hundred precepts.

Since her virtue is naturally austere through these precepts, she serves as a model for others and brings about transformation; her progress becomes ever more rapid, and she eventually transcends the three realms.
"If there are men who delight in upholding the five precepts, I will manifest before them in the body of an upāsaka and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve fulfillment.
If there are women who abide by the five precepts, I will manifest before them in the body of an upāsikā and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve fulfillment."
The five precepts are: not killing, not stealing, not engaging in sexual misconduct, not speaking falsehoods, and not drinking intoxicants.
After the Buddha had administered the Three Refuges to the householder Upāli and others among the lay community, he immediately conferred the five precepts upon them, establishing them as *upāsakas*.

The sutras state that the Five Precepts are the great prohibitions of the world. If one violates these five, in heaven one opposes the five stars; on earth one opposes the five sacred peaks; in the quarters one opposes the five emperors; and in the body one opposes the five viscera. Thus, there are immeasurable violations of worldly order resulting from such transgressions.

If one considers the supramundane perspective, this would destroy the fivefold Dharma-body and all Buddha-dharmas, because the five precepts are the root of the śīla (ethical discipline) of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.
To those who delight in studying this, one should preach this Dharma only when they appear as pure men.
The *upāsikā*—meaning a pure woman, or likewise a female lay follower (*upāsikā*).
Third, the manifestation as a female ruler in her maidenhood:

"If there are women who establish themselves through internal governance and cultivate their households and states, I appear before them in the form of a female ruler, a state lady, a titled consort, or a great matron to preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve perfection."
One who manages the internal administration of the king is called the Inner Steward (Neizai).
"Administration" (zheng) refers to that by which what is improper is rectified.

The residences of high ministers and great officers are called *jia* (houses), while those of the Son of Heaven and feudal lords are called *guo* (states). The consort of the Son of Heaven is called the Female Ruler (Nüzhu), and those of the feudal lords are called the State Ladies (Guofuren).
Regarding "those with mandates" (mingfu): when a husband is honored at court, his wife brings glory to the household.
Because she receives her mandate from the sovereign and the consort, she is called a "mandated lady.
As for "great ladies," these are women who serve as teachers to the consorts, such as Lady Hui of Cao.
Within the imperial palace and the national borders, sounds and sights increase one's indulgence; if one does not rely upon the sagely transformation, how can one aspire to pure integrity?
"If there are sentient beings who do not damage their male organ, I manifest before them in the body of a youth and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve accomplishment."

If there is a maiden who delights in remaining chaste and does not seek sexual violation, I will manifest before her in the form of a young girl and preach the Dharma for her, enabling her to achieve fulfillment.
As for young men and young women who maintain chastity beyond worldly custom and stand out among people for their character,
when the Bodhisattva dwells among them, his exhortations become even more earnest.
Fourth, regarding ghosts and spirits, there are three [categories]:
First, regarding the classes of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and gandharvas:
"If there are devas who wish to leave their celestial rank, I manifest in a celestial body to preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve success."
If there are nāgas who wish to leave their nāga status, I manifest in a nāga body to preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve fulfillment.
If there are yakṣas who wish to transcend their own class, I appear before them in a yakṣa body to preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve fulfillment.
"If a gandharva desires to be liberated from their kind, I manifest before them in the form of a gandharva and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve perfection.
Devas can weary of pleasure; nāgas can fear suffering; kumbhāṇḍas are dissolute; yakṣas are fierce and strong—each may aspire to transcend their station, yet none can be extricated except by a Sage.
Second, for those who have doubts regarding wine or belong to the class of divine serpents (*nāga*),
"If an asura wishes to be liberated from his kind, I manifest before him in the form of an asura and preach the Dharma to him, enabling him to achieve success."
If a kinnara desires to be liberated from his kind, I manifest before him in the form of a kinnara and preach the Dharma for him, enabling him to achieve realization.
If a mahoraga desires to be liberated from his kind, I manifest before him in the form of a mahoraga and preach the Dharma for him, enabling him to achieve realization.
The asuras are of hideous appearance and full of arrogance;
the kumbhāṇḍas resemble humans yet have horns; and there are those with the forms of pythons or with bellies like those of earthworms that crawl along the ground.
Because they frequently violated the precepts while practicing only meager acts of giving, they fell into these realms.
Each vows to transcend their kind, and I fulfill all their desires.
Third, regarding the various classes of beings, both human and non-human:
"If there are sentient beings who delight in being human and would cultivate the human path, I manifest in a human body and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve fulfillment."

If there are non-human beings—whether with form or without form, with perception or without perception—who delight in transcending their own kind, I manifest my body before them all and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve fulfillment.
Human existence is difficult to obtain, and it is rare to encounter a Buddha and receive his transformative teaching.
This is not because one is attached to the pleasures of heaven, but because other realms abound in suffering; therefore, one should joyfully cultivate [the path].
To possess form and the aggregate of form is like the various spirits of good and ill fortune mentioned below.
Those without form or the aggregate of consciousness are like the dispersal, dissipation, and sinking of the lower void;
those with perception but lacking the four aggregates are like the ghosts, spirits, and numina of the lower realms;
and those without perception and lacking the four aggregates are like the spirits transformed into earth, wood, metal, and stone of the lower realms.
All those above are not human beings.

These are various classes of beings with physical forms and perceptions; all such sentient creatures are included, necessarily possessing a single body that undergoes transformation according to opportunity.
Third, the conclusion.

"This is called the thirty-two kinds of wondrously pure bodies for entering lands, all of which are accomplished through the sovereign power of effortless wondrous efficacy, cultivated by the permeation of hearing through samādhi."

Through the power of illusion-like cultivation, one perfumes the stages of hearing, contemplation, and meditation to achieve the Vajra-samādhi; thus, by realizing the Truth and giving rise to its function, one attains such mastery.
Second, the fourteen fearlessnesses.

Where there is distress, he surely delivers; where there is peril, he surely rescues; where there is terror, one attains peace. He is collectively named "Fearless," taking great compassion as his essence.
The text has three parts: first, the heading.
“World-Honored One!

Furthermore, by means of this unconditioned, wondrous power of the Vajra Samādhi—cultivated through hearing and practicing what has been heard—and because I share in the same compassion and longing as all sentient beings of the six realms throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time, I cause all sentient beings to obtain fourteen kinds of merit of fearlessness within my body and mind.”

"Because one has previously realized the truth through contemplative practice and possesses its virtues, the essence gives rise to its function, enabling sentient beings to attain fourteen kinds of fearlessness.
Second, the enumeration and explanation, in four parts:
first, hearing the voice and being freed from suffering."

"First, because I do not observe myself by means of an observing subject, I cause those suffering sentient beings throughout the ten directions who contemplate my voice to immediately attain liberation."

"Because I did not observe the sounds being heard, but observed only the nature of hearing, the sounds were inherently quiescent and the characteristic of hearing was unarisen; thus, not constrained by sensory objects, I was spontaneously liberated."
Since it is so for myself, I cause all sentient beings throughout the ten directions to attain liberation from suffering upon merely hearing my voice.
Second, the elimination of calamities and misfortunes when encountering disasters, which has three parts:
first, the difficulties of the three calamities in evil lands.
"Second, by knowing and seeing the revolving restoration, one causes all sentient beings that may enter a great fire to remain unburned by the flames.
This is because the four elements originally arise from a state of profound stillness; through this revolving, they are made to become aware."
Now, returning to the fundamental state, hearing, knowledge, and vision revert to the profound stillness (*zhan*). This nature of stillness is perfectly pervasive, such that no dust can be found.
Since the fire of dust has ceased, what object could possibly burn it?
Therefore, it causes the great fires to not destroy sentient beings.
"Third, by contemplating that hearing revolves back, one causes all sentient beings who are adrift upon great waters not to be drowned by the water.
Sound has the power to wash away and toss about, like surging waves."
When hearing and seeing revolve back to the truth, the appearances of sensory objects do not arise.
When emptiness is luminous and stillness is profound, what thing can cause one to drift?
Therefore, it causes the practitioner who maintains mindfulness not to be drowned by the great waters.
"Fourth, by severing delusive thoughts and ensuring the mind is free from the intent to harm, one causes all sentient beings to enter the realms of ghosts, where the ghosts cannot harm them.

Delusive thoughts arise and perish, capable of slaying the Dharma-body and harming the life of wisdom; if confusion is severed, the true nature remains unharmed, and thus, upon entering the realm of ghosts, the ghosts cannot cause harm."

"Fifth, by perfuming the hearing until it becomes true hearing, the six sense organs are dissolved and restored, becoming identical with the faculty of sound-hearing. This can cause sentient beings, even when facing being harmed and having their bodies cut into pieces by blades, to perceive those weapons as if they were slicing through water or blowing across light; their nature remains unshaken."

By perfuming and cultivating false hearing until it becomes the true nature of hearing, the single faculty loses its opposition, and all faculties likewise merge. The water of the mind is empty and luminous, and the light of wisdom is immovable; who then is self or other that could be harmed?
Therefore, one can touch objects without obstruction, moving with ease as if wielding a sharp blade.
Second, the difficulty of ghosts, hells, and evil bandits:

"Sixth, when the clarity cultivated through hearing permeates the entire Dharma-realm, the nature of all dark obscurations cannot remain intact; it enables sentient beings such as yakṣas, rākṣasas, kumbhāṇḍas, piśācas, and pūtanas, even when they draw near, to be unable to look upon [the practitioner] with their eyes."

When the gate of cultivation through hearing and contemplation achieves lucidity and vigor, and the illumination of wisdom merges with the dharma-realm in its perfect pervasiveness, the perverse darkness of ignorance can never arise again.
Yakṣas and other such beings all receive their dark, obscured energy; since light can destroy darkness, it causes evil spirits to be unable to see with their eyes.

"Seventh, when the nature of sound is completely dissolved and the faculties of seeing and hearing turn back into the source, one becomes free from all sensory dust and delusions, such that the shackles and fetters of sentient beings cannot bind them."
"Dust-like entanglements wind around one another like imprisonment; the six sense faculties are obstructive by nature, like shackles and fetters.

Once one enters the stream and the objects of perception vanish, these bonds and obstructions can no longer be established; therefore, the one who maintains mindfulness is liberated from these shackles."
"Eighth, by extinguishing sound and perfecting hearing, one universally generates the power of compassion, enabling sentient beings to pass through perilous paths without being plundered by bandits.
Sound can plunder the mind; harming goodness constitutes a bandit."
As sounds fade and the mind becomes pure, the power of compassion permeates everywhere.
With equanimity held in the heart, good and evil are treated with the same consistency; thus, when encountering peril, bandits cannot plunder them.
Third, the difficulty of the evil mind of the three poisons.
"Ninth: when the cultivation of hearing leaves behind sensory objects, one cannot be plundered by forms; this can cause all sentient beings with excessive lust to distance themselves from greed.
Once the dust of sound has vanished and the realm of form has been extinguished, from what could thoughts of greed and desire possibly arise?"
Thus, they cause sentient beings to distance themselves from craving.

Tenth, their voices are pure and free from defilement; as the faculties and their objects are perfectly interfused, there is no longer subject and object in opposition, enabling all sentient beings who harbor anger and resentment to abandon all hatred.
Through the Samādhi of the Differentiation of Sounds, one becomes pure; since sensory objects no longer arise, the sense faculties have nothing with which to couple.
When neither favorable nor adverse conditions are encountered, the mind of anger naturally perishes; thus, it causes the practitioner to be free from all forms of hatred.

"Eleventh: when the dust is dissolved and clarity revolves, the body and mind within the dharma-realm are like lapis lazuli—luminous, penetrating, and unobstructed. This enables all those with dull natures and obstructive hindrances, including the icchantikas, to forever leave behind the darkness of doubt."
Dust and darkness were eliminated, and true illumination immediately returned; the world, the body, and the mind became transparently clear and unimpeded.
All is but awakening—what, then, constitutes delusion and darkness?
Thus, he causes those of icchantika nature to all give rise to true faith.
Third, responding to requests according to their desires: "Twelfth, his form melts and returns to hearing;

unmoving from the site of enlightenment, he enters into the mundane world. Without destroying the world, he is able to pervade the ten directions, making offerings to Buddhas as numerous as motes of dust. At the side of each Buddha, he serves as a Dharma Prince. He can cause those sentient beings within the Dharma realm who lack sons and desire a male child to give birth to a son endowed with merit and wisdom."

The obstructive forms are integrated and transformed back into true hearing; thus, without moving from the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), one enters into the worlds. One’s body is limitless, reaching throughout the ten directions, continuing the lineage of the Dharma King without interruption. Because of the power of samādhi and the perfection of merit and wisdom, those who seek a son shall have their wishes fulfilled without fail.

"Thirteenth: The six sense organs are perfectly penetrating; their luminous illumination is non-dual and encompasses the worlds of the ten directions. This establishes the Great Perfect Mirror, the Empty Tathāgata-garbha, which receives and upholds the secret Dharma gates of the Buddhas as numerous as motes of dust throughout the ten directions without loss. It can cause those beings within the Dharma-realm who have no children and desire daughters to give birth to daughters who are upright, virtuous, gentle, compliant, beloved by all people, and endowed with auspicious marks."

The six sense faculties are perfectly pervasive, interpenetrating and illuminating; they contain and manifest the single, precious awakening of the ten directions as non-dual and undifferentiated—this is called the Great Perfect Mirror.
Furthermore, it can accord with and serve all Buddhas as numerous as motes of dust, receiving and containing immeasurable Dharma gates without loss or decay—this is called the Treasury of Space.

Possessing the virtues of a woman and the grace of a consort, she provides for life and practices obedience; being gentle, intelligent, chaste, and upright, with all auspicious marks perfectly complete—through such thoughts and aspirations, she is able to give birth.
4. Attaining Merit by Reciting the Name. "Fourteenth:

Within this trichiliocosm, there are currently sixty-two *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* (Ganges-sand) numbers of Dharma Princes who dwell in the world among the ten billion suns and moons. They cultivate the Dharma and establish models to teach and transform sentient beings; their skillful means and wisdom in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings are each different."
The "many beings" referred to are the skillful means (upāya), which is the provisional;
wisdom (prajñā) is the ultimate reality.
The lower [category] can be compared to one name:

"By means of the fundamental root of perfect penetration that I have attained, I gave rise to the wondrous gateway of the ear; thereafter, my body and mind became subtle and wondrously inclusive, pervading the entire Dharma-realm."
The reason for this has been stated previously.
That which Avalokiteśvara cultivates enters through the three types of wisdom (*prajñā*); this is the root of all practices.

Since every Buddha expounds the teaching by means of sound, and every sentient being attains realization through hearing, who can emerge from the world without relying on the body? Who does not follow this path?
How much more so, then, can one transcend all apprehension regarding the object of sound, untie the knots of the sense faculties, and return to the true limit?
The primordial luminosity of the mind is wondrous; the realms of the one and the many are interpenetrated.
The fundamental stillness of awakening is perfect; the designations of "self" and "other" are equal.
Because all bodies are one body, it is said that they are "subtle and all-encompassing";
because one body is all bodies, it is said that they "pervade the Dharma-realm.
This is precisely the reason for [the attainment of] merit and so forth.
"If one can cause sentient beings to uphold my name, their merit shall be exactly equal and no different from that of those sixty-two Ganges-sands of Dharma princes who uphold it together."
“World-Honored One!
My single name is no different from those many names; it is because I have cultivated this that I have attained true perfect penetration.
This is analogous to the equality of merit and so forth.
This means that by virtue of the principle of equality through one's own realization, one subsequently enables others to attain equal merit.
This concludes the reason for the preceding section.
Third, the conclusion.
"These are called the fourteen powers of bestowing fearlessness, through which blessings are fully provided for all sentient beings," as the text states.

Third, the inconceivable virtues and functions are so transcendent that they exceed the reach of words and intellect; this reveals the characteristics of the merits of the essence of the Great Perfect Mirror.
However, the power and function of these merits are one in essence; that which is internalized is called "merit" (guṇa), while that which is externally applied is called "function" (vṛtti).

Although previously he manifested responses according to the capacities of beings, governing things as required by the occasion to uproot suffering and bestow happiness, such instances remained limited in number. Yet, his virtues of sovereign transformation—which are manifest everywhere, wondrous beyond compare, and inconceivable—have not yet been fully set forth; therefore, they are described now.
The text has two parts:
first, the formal presentation:
"World-Honored One!"

"Furthermore, because I have attained this perfect penetration and cultivated the realization of the Unsurpassed Way, I am also able to skillfully attain the four inconceivable, effortless, and wondrous virtues.
If internal virtue is not full, external function will not arise."

By perfuming the four original immeasurable minds with the vajra-samādhi, one realizes the fruit through which actual virtues manifest; thus, the four matters are accomplished, appearing spontaneously and inconceivably.
2. Detailed Explanation, in four parts:
1. Manifesting Forms and Preaching the Dharma.

"First, because I initially attained the wondrous and subtle mind of hearing, the essence of the mind left behind all hearing; seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing could no longer be separated, becoming a single, perfectly integrated, pure, and precious awakening."
This describes the fundamental source of virtue.
The nature of hearing is fundamentally true; it is neither coarse nor subtle. Because it is free from all relative distinctions, it is called "subtle-subtle.
That which is not coarse is termed "refined," and that which is detached from characteristics is termed "abandoned."
When one faculty returns to its source, all six faculties are simultaneously liberated; therefore, they do not remain partitioned, but become a single precious awakening.
As it says in the passage below:
"Therefore, I am able to manifest many wondrous forms and am able to preach boundless secret spiritual mantras."
This is the signpost.
Its wondrous forms appear in manifold ways and cannot be constrained by physical measurement;
its secret mantras are boundless and cannot be grasped through verbal expression.

This is because, through the power of samādhi, one perfumes the original immeasurable mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī-apramāṇa-citta*), manifesting various forms and proclaiming various mantras, so that all who see or hear them may obtain sublime bliss.

"Among them, some manifest one head, three heads, five heads, seven heads, nine heads, eleven heads, and so on, up to one hundred and eight heads, a thousand heads, ten thousand heads, and eighty-four thousand śakara heads."

With two arms, four arms, six arms, eight arms, ten arms, twelve arms, fourteen, sixteen, eighteen, twenty, up to twenty-four; and so on, even unto one hundred and eight arms, a thousand arms, ten thousand arms, and eighty-four thousand mudrā-arms.
Two eyes, three eyes, four eyes, nine eyes, and so on up to one hundred and eight eyes, a thousand eyes, ten thousand eyes, and eighty-four thousand pure jewel eyes.
Whether through compassion or majesty, whether through meditative concentration or wisdom, one rescues and protects sentient beings, attaining great mastery.
That which stands foremost among all sages is the Dharma-body (dharmakāya).
The arm capable of lifting and supporting others is the Transformation-body (nirmāṇakāya).
The eyes guide clarity; they are the body of wisdom.
Since no object is seen in vain and every sight necessarily brings benefit, one is thus able to provide rescue and protection.
Second, there are fearless sentient beings.

"Second, because I have been liberated from the six sense-objects through hearing and reflection, just as sound passes through a wall without obstruction, I am able to manifest every single form and recite every single mantra with wondrous skill. These forms and mantras can bestow fearlessness upon all sentient beings; therefore, throughout the lands of the ten directions, as numerous as motes of dust, I am known as the Bestower of Fearlessness."

"By means of the power of illusion, which permeates their original universal compassion, they are able to manifest infinite bodies from a single body and a single body from infinite bodies, appearing in every land throughout the ten directions, even within a mote of dust."
As each mantra was spoken, it extracted all sufferings and afflictions; fearless sentient beings attained great sovereignty.
Third, "Relinquishing Jewels to Seek Pity":

"Third, because I have cultivated the fundamental, wondrous, perfect, and penetrating root of purity, in all the worlds I traverse, I cause sentient beings to relinquish their bodies and precious treasures to seek my compassion."

"By the power of samādhi, which perfumes the fundamental mind of joy, all sentient beings who see them as they travel through the worlds will give rise to delight; they will not begrudge their bodies or wealth in seeking to evoke compassion."
Fourth, obtaining whatever one seeks according to one’s desires:

"Fourth, having attained the Buddha-mind and realized ultimate fruition, I am able to offer various precious treasures as offerings to the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, extending also to all sentient beings within the six realms of the Dharma-realm. If they seek a wife, they obtain a wife; if they seek a son, they obtain a son; if they seek samādhi, they obtain samādhi; if they seek long life, they obtain long life; and so on, even up to seeking great nirvāṇa, they obtain great nirvāṇa."

Through the power of perfect illumination, one perfumes the original mind of relinquishment; subsequently, upon attaining the fruit of realization, one is able to bestow precious treasures upon the Buddhas above and extend them to sentient beings below, ensuring that all sought-after mundane and supramundane dharmas are fulfilled according to one's vows.

Regarding the two preceding sections on joy (*muditā*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*), either may be applied to either. Furthermore, to correlate the preceding passages as a whole with the three contemplations:

because of the contemplation that merges appearances and clarifies the spirit, cessation (*śānti*) manifests before one; because of the contemplation that gives rise to illusions to eliminate defilements, one attains the two kinds of excellence; and because of the contemplation of the numinous mind that transcends all dependencies, there are the four inconceivables. These are also the contemplations of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), provisionality (*prajñapti*), and the Middle Way (*madhyamā*), as can be seen in detail from the text.
III. Summary and Conclusion, in two parts: A.
Concluding the answer to the question:

"Regarding the Buddha’s inquiry into perfect penetration, I attained the Samādhi of Universal Illumination through the gateway of the ear. By attaining mastery over the conditioned mind and entering the phase of the 'flowing-in,' I achieved *samāpatti* and realized Bodhi; this is the foremost method."
The Samādhi of Perfect Illumination is identical to the Samādhi of One Practice.

This means that when one first takes the true reality as the object, the created realm is immediately the Middle Way; there is nothing that is not true. By binding the conditions to the Dharma-realm and contemplating the Dharma-realm in a single thought-moment, it is said that "the mind of conditions is sovereign."

This is precisely the Śūraṅgama-samādhi that is the primary tenet of this sutra; it is the true and perfect penetration praised by Mañjuśrī, and the light of all Buddhas intersects to celebrate this teaching together.
May those of later generations, upon reaching this point, fortunately take heed and not regard it as merely casual.
2. Narrating the Praise for Receiving the Name.

"World-Honored One, that Buddha-Tathāgata praised me for having well attained the Dharma-gate of Perfect Penetration. In the midst of the great assembly, he conferred upon me the name Avalokiteśvara; because I contemplate and listen to the perfect luminosity of the ten directions, the name 'Avalokiteśvara' pervades the worlds of the ten directions."

"Visualizing with the eyes and listening with the ears"—this briefly cites two of the six sense faculties. When one visualizes this or listens to sounds, the functions of the single faculty revolve back upon themselves and the sixfold operations cease to exist. Therefore, the perfect luminosity of the ten directions is but the single precious awakening; it is from this that its name is derived, and it likewise pervades all things.
I. Praising the inconceivable teaching, which primarily concerns Avalokiteśvara while incidentally including other sages.
This section has four parts;
the first is "The Mutual Radiance of All Buddhas."

At that time, from his five limbs, the World-Honored One simultaneously emitted precious light, which reached far to moisten the crowns of the heads of the Tathāgatas as numerous as motes of dust throughout the ten directions, as well as the Dharma Princes and all the Bodhisattvas.

Those Tathāgatas likewise emitted precious light from their five limbs; from every direction, even as small as a mote of dust, it came to pour over the crown of the Buddha’s head, as well as upon the great Bodhisattvas and Arhats in the assembly.
The forest trees and ponds all resound with the sounds of the Dharma; their interlacing lights entwine like a net of precious threads.
The faculty of hearing is perfectly penetrating, encompassing all five faculties; it accords with the Buddhas, and the descriptions of its realization are identical.

As for the great Bodhisattvas and Arhats, these are the twenty-five sages previously mentioned who expounded their methods of perfect penetration; since it was sealed that all were indeed non-deviant perfect penetrations, precious light was emitted and poured over their crowns.

The forest trees and ponds that proclaim the sounds of the Dharma are already designated as "Perfect Penetration" (*yuantong*); since both self and other are equally permeated by them, their wisdom encompasses all things—what Dharma would they not proclaim?
Their interlacing light forms a net, perfectly spreading the Great Teaching.
Second, the great assembly receives benefit.
This entire assembly attains what they have never experienced before; all universally obtain the Vajra Samādhi.

Hearing the Perfect Contemplation with their ears and touching the Light of Wisdom with their crowns, they simultaneously attain the Samādhi of Avalokiteśvara. Thus, these twenty-four sages assemble together at the single gate of Avalokiteśvara, and all are named as having attained the Vajra Samādhi.
Third, the Adornment of the Realm by Raining Flowers.

At that moment, the heavens rained down lotus flowers of a hundred jewels—intermingled and variegated in blue, yellow, red, and white. The empty space of the ten directions became the color of the seven treasures; the body of the Dharma was pristine and pure, surpassing all that the devas and nāgas could conceive.
Now it shall be manifested: like a jewel-adorned void, it is the integration of myriad practices; thus, flowers are interspersed therein.
Fourth, the sound is proclaimed throughout the entire land:

in this Sahā world, the great earth, mountains, and rivers all simultaneously disappear, and one sees only the lands of the ten directions, as numerous as motes of dust, merging into a single realm, where the chanting of Brahma-songs and melodic hymns are spontaneously performed.
When the faculties and their objects are dissolved and restored, the Dharma-realm is perfectly realized; thus, mountains and rivers no longer appear, merging into a single realm.
*Brahma* means "pure"; its full form is *Vandana*, correctly *Vaśī*, which is translated here as "praise."
IV. The Buddha’s Command for Mañjuśrī to Discern; Part Three: A.
The Buddha’s Command to Mañjuśrī; Part Two: 1.
Pointing to the Teaching to Reveal Their Identity.
Thereupon, the Tathāgata addressed Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince:

"Observe now these twenty-five great Bodhisattvas and Arhats who have no more to learn, each of whom has spoken of the expedient means by which they first attained the Way. They all say that they cultivated true and perfect penetration; in their respective practices, there is truly no distinction of superiority or inferiority, nor of priority or posteriority."
"The essence of spiritual practice is to take the realization of reality as its goal; since all have now attained realization, there is no distinction of superior or inferior.
Nevertheless, because days and kalpas differ by factors of ten million, distinctions of prior and subsequent arise."
Alternatively, one may attain the respective state by approaching each of them individually, with no distinction between before and after.
Second, one should select [the teaching] according to the faculties:
"I now wish to bring Ānanda to enlightenment; among these twenty-five practices, which one corresponds to his faculty?"
Furthermore, after my parinirvāṇa, by what skillful means can sentient beings in this world who have entered the Bodhisattva vehicle and seek the unsurpassed path most easily achieve success?
If they enter through the three categories, the seven elements, or various specialized paths according to their individual faculties, these are all skillful means.

If this teaching were to be propagated throughout this realm across the present and future, such that those of superior, middling, and inferior capacities could all attain realization and entry, serving as a perpetual means for sentient beings to achieve the Way—among these twenty-five gates, which would be the most excellent?

Because he previously requested from the Tathāgatas of the ten directions the initial expedient for attaining the wondrous samādhi of bodhi, he now causes him to select a universal dharma-gate so that he may achieve accomplishment.
I. Exposition by means of verses, in two parts: A.
Paying homage in accordance with the imperial decree.

Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince, having received the Buddha’s compassionate command, immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and, sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, spoke these verses in response to the Buddha:

Mañjuśrī, sovereign of wisdom and virtue, whose speech and actions are unfathomable and whose discernment is beyond doubt, causes all to fall silent when he grants or takes away their hearts' inclinations; thus, receiving the Buddha’s command, I respectfully speak these verses.
II. The actual exposition of the verses, in three parts:
A. Verses on the dual sources of the true and the deluded, in two parts:
1. A brief clarification of the true and the deluded.
In selecting the gates of practice, one first clarifies the distinction between the true and the delusive. If there were neither delusion nor awakening, how could there be spiritual cultivation?
It is because one becomes deluded regarding the One True Reality that all manner of delusions arise; yet, as things do not remain forever obstructed, there is a time for awakening.

Awakening follows the various gates of the faculties, thereby resulting in differences of speed; the ultimate limit of awakening is called Great Nirvana. Therefore, the text below states: "The wondrous nature is perfectly luminous and free from all names and marks. Originally, there were no worlds or sentient beings; it is due to delusion that they arise, and because of their arising that there is cessation. Arising and cessation are termed 'delusion,' while the extinction of delusion is termed 'truth. These are known as the two designations for the Tathāgata’s reliance upon transformation: Bodhi and Nirvana."
Therefore, this is clarified first.
The text has three parts;
the first is: The Sole True Source.
"The nature of the ocean of awakening is clear and perfect; this perfect clarity is the fundamental subtlety of awakening.

This reveals the ocean of the one true nature, which is beyond names and free from marks, neither real nor delusory, neither awakened nor deluded—a single, perfectly constant reality from which nothing else can be obtained. This is what is meant by the "wondrous nature's perfect luminosity," which is devoid of all names and marks, and wherein, from the beginning, there have been no worlds or sentient beings.
The nature of awakening is all-pervasive, profoundly deep and tranquil; thus, it is like the ocean.
The following phrase is a further exclamation: it is inconceivable and transcends all dualistic opposition; therefore, it is called "wondrous."
2. Delusion arising from causes, in two parts:
1. Clarifying the actual arising of delusion:
"Originally, luminous clarity gave rise to the object; once the object was established, the nature of luminous clarity perished."

The essence of perfect, clear awareness is originally luminous and illuminating; because deluded awareness fails to comprehend this, it takes it as an object. Once the object is falsely established, the deluded subject arises. From that which is ultimately non-existent, there is formed what is ultimately existent; therefore, it is called "the arising of the object," not that it arises from the True.
Once the characteristic of darkness appears, the nature of clarity is immediately obscured; because it is obscured, it is said to have perished.
"From delusive ignorance comes empty space; based on space, the world is established. As thought settles, the land is formed; as perception arises, sentient beings come into being."
"When the world first arises, a state of inert emptiness appears first; because it is produced from deluded thought, it is said that 'delusive error exists.
As stated in the following passage: 'Even up to empty space, all are produced by deluded thought.'"

Regarding the establishment of the world-system upon emptiness: the substance of the world-system consists of the four wheels, all of which exist in dependence upon emptiness. As stated in the preceding text: "Awakened clarity and empty dullness interact to produce agitation; thus there is the wind-wheel that supports the world-system," and so forth.

Deluded thoughts coalesce to form the external land, and the deluded mind’s perceptions form the internal sentient beings; once both the environment and its inhabitants are manifested, they are collectively termed the "world.
Second, the explanation by means of an applied metaphor.
"Empty space arises within the Great Enlightenment, like a single bubble emerging from the sea; the minute dust-like lands of the outflows are all produced in dependence upon empty space.
Empty space is dark and dull; its essence is non-awakening. That non-awakening gives rise to awakening, just as a single bubble emerges from the sea.
The *Awakening of Faith* states: "It is precisely because of awakening that there is non-awakening.

The subsequent passage says: "You should know that empty space arises within your mind, like a fragment of cloud appearing in the vast clarity of the great sky; how much more so, then, are the various worlds contained within empty space?"
The dharma and its metaphor are thus evident.
Second, returning to the truth by reversing delusion:
"When the bubble is extinguished, even emptiness is fundamentally non-existent; how much more so the various realms of the three existences?"

The subsequent passage states: "If even one among you were to give rise to true realization and return to the source, the voids of the ten directions would all be dissolved; how then could the lands within that void not tremble and split apart?"

"Because delusion fundamentally lacks a root and ultimately does not arise, empty space is like a bubble—extinguished without being extinguished; the three realms of existence are like an illusion—non-existent without being non-existent."
II. Differences and Similarities in Practice and Realization, in two parts:
A. Identity in Principle, Difference in Practice:
"The nature of returning to the source is non-dual, yet the expedient means have many gates."
They all return to a single principle, and that principle is without distinction.
Yet, in practice there are partiality and perfection, and progress is neither uniform nor equal in speed.

The *Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna* states: "The unsurpassed, wondrous enlightenment pervades the ten directions; it gives birth to the Tathāgatas and is of the same essence as all phenomena, equal and without duality. In accordance with various practices, its expedient means are immeasurable."
2. The Sages are the same while the ordinary are different.

"The nature of the sages is all-pervasive; whether following or reversing [the path], everything is a skillful means. When those with the initial resolve enter samādhi, their progress—whether slow or fast—is not of the same order."

If a noble person’s faculties are such that they have already realized the state of a noble one, they may enter awakening through either the direct or the reverse order, with no further distinction of depth.
Because this concerns the initial entry into the Path, it is necessary to select [the appropriate method] so that progress may be swift.

As stated above: "The Tathāgatas of the ten directions practice within each of the eighteen realms and all attain the perfect, unsurpassed Bodhi; among them, there is neither superiority nor inferiority."
"However, you are of inferior capacity and have not yet attained sovereign wisdom within this [samādhi]; therefore, I proclaim it so that you may enter deeply through a single gate.
*Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra Commentary*, Fascicle Six, Part One.
